title: Server-First HCI
text:
Pre-print preview. A draft of Server-First HCI published for review. Every chapter is drafted; none is final. Corrections are welcome, and the preface says how the book is made.






Preface
This book teaches one way to build a web interface and one way to find out whether people can use it. The interface is server-rendered HTML that works with JavaScript off and is enhanced with HTMX where that helps. The evaluation is a short cycle of instrumentation, pilots with consenting participants, analysis, a redesign and a check that the redesign worked. A single task-list application carries the reader from the first page to the last, and every line of code in the text is included from a tagged repository that compiles.
It is written for second-year undergraduates who can already program and have not yet built for people other than themselves. The code is Kotlin and Ktor; the prose stays away from the language wherever it can, because the argument about hypermedia, accessibility and evidence does not depend on it, and a Python edition is planned. A reader outside a university who wants the same material can work through the chapters in order and ignore the module overlay.
The module overlay is a separate part, rendered only with the module profile, that turns the twelve chapters into a six-week strand of two labs a week. It holds the schedule, the assessment and one page of institution-specific detail; nothing else in the book names a week, a deadline or a university. A department adopting the strand edits that one page and leaves the chapters alone.

title: 1  Server-first
text:
1.1 Why the server renders the page
You clone a working task list, read how a request becomes a page, and fill the one gap left in it; by the end the list adds and deletes tasks with JavaScript off, and the same page works enhanced with HTMX.
Before you start, work through Appendix A until ./gradlew build passes on your machine, then check out the tag this chapter is written against: git checkout week-06-start. If you have not written Kotlin before, read Appendix B; this chapter assumes you can read a function and a map literal and nothing more. You have met HTML and CSS once, which is enough.
The application in this book sends the browser finished HTML. The browser shows it without running a script, and every link and form on it works with JavaScript off. HTMX is then added as a layer on top: a small script that lets a form or link fetch a fragment of HTML and swap it into the page instead of reloading. If the script fails to load, is blocked, or is switched off, the page is still the page.
This is progressive enhancement, and the GOV.UK service manual requires it for government services (Government Digital Service, no date). Hypermedia Systems makes the longer argument for building this way (Gross, Stepinski and Akşimşek, 2023). The reason this book takes the position is narrower: the HTML the server sends is the HTML a screen reader reads, so there is one place to get the structure, the labels and the announcements right, and one place to check them.
Every interaction in the task list is therefore reached two ways: a plain form submission that ends in a redirect, and an HTMX request that ends in a fragment. The server tells them apart by one request header, and every handler answers both.

Commit with a message that says what was added. title: 2  Needs-finding and consent
text:
2.1 Why ask people
By the end you have a consent process you can run, notes from your first interviews, five or six job stories, and a backlog in which every row points at the evidence for it.
Before you start, read Appendix F, which holds the data-protection principles this chapter relies on, and have the consent form from Appendix H to hand. You need one other person to interview and about two hours. Nothing in this chapter touches the code.
A requirement names a solution: "the system shall allow users to filter tasks by status". A need names a situation and what the person in it is trying to do: "when I am preparing for a review, I want to see only the tasks I have to hand in, so I can check I have not missed one". Solutions date and needs do not. If you know the need, you can change the solution when the evidence or the technology changes, and you can tell when a solution has not worked.
The job story is the form this book uses to write a need down (Klement, 2013). It has four parts: a situation, a motivation, an outcome, and the constraint behind them.
An example from the application you built in Chapter 1:
Compare the persona form: "As a blind user, I want screen reader support so I can use the app." It puts a label where the situation should be, assumes everyone under the label needs the same thing, and says nothing about why. The job story is specific about the moment, and that specificity covers people the label leaves out. Someone whose trackpad broke this morning is, for today, navigating by keyboard, and the story about keyboard access is theirs as well.

title: 2  Needs-finding and consent
text:
2.2 Consent first
You are about to write down what another person says about their working life. That is personal data, however small the interview, and the rules in Appendix F apply. Three of them bite here. Collect the minimum: no names, no student numbers, no email addresses; a pseudonym such as P1 in their place. Say where the notes will be kept and when they will be deleted, and keep to it. Tell the participant they can stop at any point, see their notes, or have them deleted, and tell them how to ask.
For a short interview between classmates, with no recording and no identifying data, spoken consent is enough, provided you have said what you will do before you start. Copy the consent form in Appendix H into your repository as research/consent-form.md, fill the contact fields in from your institution's page, and read it to your participant or hand it to them. Record the date, the pseudonym you assigned, and that consent was given. Nothing else about the participant goes in the file. The fuller participant information sheet in Appendix G is for the pilots in Chapter 8, where you will be timing people; it is more than this exercise needs.
If you find yourself typing a participant's name into the notes to tidy up later, stop and replace it now. A name committed to a git history is a name you cannot promise to delete.

title: 2  Needs-finding and consent
text:
2.3 Activity 1: interview your partner
Pair up. Each of you interviews the other for ten minutes, then you swap. If there is time, find a third person. Use these prompts, in your own words, and let the answer run before you move on.

Tell me about the last time you used a to-do list or task manager. What were you trying to get done?
What frustrates you most about keeping track of tasks? Can you give me a specific time it happened?
Have you ever lost track of something important? What happened?
Do you ever work without a mouse or trackpad, on a train, or when something has broken? How does that change how you use things?
Have you tried to use something like this with your eyes closed, or in bright sunlight? What was hard?
If you could change one thing to make this less stressful, what would it be?

When an answer is short, ask "can you tell me more about that?", "what did you do instead?", or "how did that feel?". When the participant describes a feature they would like, ask what they were doing when they wanted it; the feature is their solution, and you want the situation underneath. When they say nothing frustrates them, ask about the last deadline they nearly missed.
Keep the notes in research/notes.md, one heading per participant and one subheading per prompt. Under each prompt write three things: what they said, as close to their words as you can manage; what you noticed, including hesitation or a workaround they described; and one or two theme tags from a short vocabulary you agree with your partner beforehand, such as confirmation, keyboard, contrast, filter, progress. Keep a quotation and your reading of it visibly distinct. The quotation is evidence; your reading is a claim about it.

title: 2  Needs-finding and consent
text:
2.4 Activity 2: write job stories
Read both sets of notes together. List each situation in which someone struggled, the need behind it, and where in the notes it came from. Then write five or six job stories in research/stories.md, numbered S1 onward. Each story has the four lines above, the evidence (participant and line number in the notes), who else the situation catches (a person using a screen reader, navigating by keyboard, with low vision, under cognitive load, or with a motor impairment), and the WCAG 2.2 success criterion it maps to where there is one (W3C, 2023). The criteria this book uses, by number and level, are listed in Chapter 4; look ahead to it now.
Two things go wrong at this step. If both participants said the same thing, that is one story with two pieces of evidence, not two stories. If a story comes from your own testing rather than an interview, such as the no-JavaScript path giving no feedback after a redirect, write it anyway and record the evidence as your own observation. The backlog treats the two kinds of evidence differently, so the distinction has to survive.

2.5 Activity 3: build the backlog
The backlog is a CSV file at backlog/backlog.csv. Its header is defined here and nowhere else; later chapters add rows to it and never change the columns.
id,title,story_ref,story_type,need,type,severity,inclusion_risk,evidence,notes,candidate_fix







Column
Holds




id
A number, unique within the file.


title
Under ten words.


story_ref
stories.md#S2, or notes.md#L15 for an item straight from the notes.


story_type
job story, observation, or audit for an item that will come from Chapter 4.

The need in a phrase: "confirmation", "keyboard access".

accessibility, usability, or technical.


severity

inclusion_risk
Who is caught, comma-separated: screen reader, keyboard, low vision, cognitive, motor.

The notes reference, a WCAG criterion number, or own observation.

Anything that explains the row.

Aim for eight rows, mixing stories from the interviews with what you noticed building the application in Chapter 1. One row in full, to set the pattern:
2,No confirmation after submitting the add form without JavaScript,stories.md#S2,job story,confirmation,accessibility,high,"cognitive,screen reader",P1 notes L12; P2 notes L8,The HTMX path announces a status; the redirect path says nothing,true
To choose the candidate fixes, score each row. Severity scores three for high, two for medium, one for low. Add one if more than one group is caught. Add two if the row is a Level A failure and one if it is Level AA. The row above scores five: high severity, two groups, and 4.1.3 at AA. A cosmetic row that catches one group and maps to no criterion scores one. Mark one or two of the highest-scoring rows candidate_fix=true, provided each can be fixed in an hour or two and has a criterion to check it against afterwards. Chapter 9 adds the cost of a fix to this scoring once you have measured something; until then, severity and inclusion are enough to choose by.
A row with an empty evidence cell is an opinion. Keep it if you want to, but it does not become a candidate fix.

Commit research/consent-form.md, research/notes.md, research/stories.md and backlog/backlog.csv. Check that no file contains a name, a student number or an email address other than your own. Pick one row and trace it from the notes to the story to the backlog; whatever you cannot trace is what the evidence chain will need before the assessment.

title: 3  Inline edit
text:
3.1 Activity 1: two templates for one row
By the end a task can be renamed in place by mouse, by keyboard and by screen reader, with one route serving both the HTMX partial and the full page.
Before you start, commit your work from Chapter 1 and check out week-07-lab1; git describe --tags prints the tag name when you are on it. Have a screen reader you can start (Appendix E says how for Windows, macOS and Linux) and keep Appendix D open for the attributes.
Inline edit is the pattern where a row turns into a form and back again without leaving the page. It is harder to get right than add or delete because a row now has three states, viewing, editing and editing with an error, and each of them has to work in both modes and keep the keyboard focus somewhere sensible. The tag has the finished feature; this chapter reads it, then checks it with a mouse, a keyboard and a screen reader. If you would rather build it than read it, start from week-06, take the tests from this tag with git checkout week-07-lab1 -- src/test, and use the code below as the target.
A row in view mode is _item.peb. At this tag it has three controls.
All three are buttons inside forms, so a person using a keyboard or a screen reader meets the same kind of control three times, and each button is described by the task title through aria-describedby. The Edit form is a GET with a hidden edit field: without JavaScript it lands on /tasks?edit=<id>, which is the list page with that one row in edit mode; with HTMX it fetches /tasks/<id>/edit and swaps the fragment over the <li>. The mark done form POSTs to /tasks/<id>/toggle and swaps the row back in with its new state; the button's text says which way the toggle will go.
A row in edit mode is _edit.peb.
The <li> keeps the same id, so an outerHTML swap in either direction replaces exactly one row. The field has a visible label tied by for, and the label, hint and error all carry the task id so the ids stay unique when two rows are on the page. autofocus puts the cursor in the field: the browser does this on a full page load, and HTMX does it when it swaps in content that carries the attribute. After a failed save the field is marked aria-invalid="true" and the error paragraph is added to its aria-describedby, so a screen reader reads the error when the field is focused, and the paragraph has role="alert" so it is read when it appears. Cancel is a plain link to the list, enhanced with an hx-get that fetches the view row.
The list page chooses between the two.
editingId is set only when the URL carries edit, so at most one row is a form.

title: 3  Inline edit
section: 3.3 Activity 3: check it three ways and in two modes
text:
3.3 Activity 3: check it three ways and in two modes
Start the server and add two tasks. With the mouse, press Edit on one, change the title, press Save: the row swaps back and the status box says it was saved. Press Edit again and Cancel: the original row returns, unchanged. Blank the field and Save: the row stays a form, the field has a red border, the message is under it, and the status box repeats the message.
Now the keyboard. Press Tab from the address bar until the first Edit button has focus and press Enter. Focus should land in the title field with the cursor in it; if it lands nowhere and you are back at the top of the page, the response was a full page rather than the fragment, which means the request went out without the header. Type a title and press Enter: a form with one text field submits on Enter, so Save needs no click. Tab to Cancel and press Enter; Tab to Mark done and press Space.
Then the screen reader. Navigate to the Edit button: you should hear "Edit" and the task title, from aria-describedby. Press it and listen: the field announces as "Title", an edit field, with the hint. Blank it and save: you should hear the message twice, once as the alert appears and once as the status region changes. Save a valid title: you should hear it was saved. Write down what you heard at each of the three points; a screen reader that stays silent at one of them is a finding, and Chapter 4 says what to do with it. If the error is read when it appears but not when you return to the field, the id in aria-describedby and the id on the paragraph disagree.
Last, the other mode. From a second terminal, with <id> copied from a row's id attribute in the page source:
curl -i http://localhost:8080/tasks/<id>/edit
curl -i -d 'title=' http://localhost:8080/tasks/<id>/edit
The first prints a 303 whose Location is /tasks?edit=<id>; the second a 303 whose Location ends error=blank_title&title=. Open each Location in the browser and you see the list page with that row as a form, the second with the error shown. Then switch JavaScript off (the click paths for two browsers are in Chapter 6) and go through the same three flows: Edit reloads the page with the row as a form, Save reloads it as a row, Cancel is a link back to the list, and the address bar shows the state at every step. If after a successful save the form is still open, the redirect carried edit; a success goes to tasksPath() with no arguments.
Two things about focus differ between the modes and are not defects. After an HTMX swap the focus is wherever the new markup puts it, here the field; after a reload the browser honours autofocus the same way, and the page scrolls to the top first. The focus was checked in both modes by driving a browser against the tag; the scroll was not. And a page can carry only one autofocus, which editingId guarantees.

title: 4  Auditing and fixing
text:
4.1 Activity 1: the automated pass
By the end you have audited the task list against WCAG 2.2, recorded each defect against its criterion, and fixed one of them with a diff you can explain.
Before you start, commit your work and check out week-07-lab2-audit; git describe --tags prints the name when you are on it. Install the axe DevTools extension in Chrome, Edge or Firefox from the browser's extension store (Deque Systems, no date), and have a screen reader you can start (Appendix E). Open backlog/backlog.csv from Chapter 2.
This tag is not the code you left at the end of Chapter 3. Four or so accessibility defects were added to it in one commit, with no comment in the code pointing at them. Some are the kind an automated checker reports in a second; some are found only by a person using a keyboard or a screen reader. The point of the lab is the method, which is four passes and a backlog row per finding, and the method is the same one you run on your own work from here to the end of the book.
Start the server, open the list, and add two or three tasks so the page has rows. Open the developer tools (F12), find the axe DevTools tab (it may be behind the >> overflow menu), and press "Scan ALL of my page". The results are grouped by rule. Each one names the rule, shows the element it fired on, links to an explanation, and lists the WCAG success criteria it maps to. axe also labels each issue critical, serious, moderate or minor; those are the tool's own words for impact, not WCAG levels, and the backlog uses WCAG's.
Record every issue as a backlog row now, before you judge it: story_type is audit, evidence is the axe rule name and the criterion number with its level, and title says where on the page it is. If the scan reports nothing at all, check git describe --tags, and check that the tab you scanned is the list and not the 404 page.
An automated checker reads the DOM. It can tell that a field has no label, that an image has no alternative, that two colours are too close, and that an element has an attribute pointing at an id that does not exist. It cannot tell whether an announcement was made, whether a label's text makes sense, or where the focus went after a swap. The other three passes are for those.

Put the mouse out of reach. Click once in the address bar, then press Tab and keep pressing it, and watch where the focus goes. The first stop is the skip link, which should appear when it has focus and move you to the main content when you press Enter. After that every control on the page should be reached in the order it is read, each should show a visible focus ring, Enter should activate a button or a link, and Space should activate a button. Go through the add flow, the edit flow and a delete this way. Press Escape and Shift-Tab a few times to check nothing holds the focus.

4.3 Activity 3: the screen reader pass
Start one screen reader: NVDA on Windows, VoiceOver on macOS, Orca on Linux. The keys for starting it, reading the page, and moving by heading and by form field are in Appendix E; this chapter only says what to listen for. Read the page from the top once. Then move through the headings: you should hear the page title, then the add section and the list section. Then move through the form fields: each should be announced with a name, its type, and its hint; a field announced as "edit text" with no name has no label. Add a task and listen for the status region. Submit a blank title and listen for the error. Move through the links and images, listening for a link with no text and an image announced by its file name or as "unlabelled graphic". Move to each button and listen for which task it belongs to.

4.4 Activity 4: the contrast pass
Inspect a piece of text with the developer tools and click the colour swatch next to its color in the Styles pane. The picker shows the contrast ratio against the background and whether it meets AA and AAA. Check body text, each kind of button, the status box, the error text, the link in the footer and the focus ring. The WebAIM contrast checker does the same from two hex values (WebAIM, no date). Text needs 4.5 to 1, or 3 to 1 if it is large; the parts of a control you need to see to use it, including the focus ring, need 3 to 1.








What you are measuring
Criterion
Level




Text against its background
1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum)
AA


Control boundaries, states and focus indicators against their surroundings
1.4.11 Non-text Contrast
AA



Two things look wrong at this tag and are not. The Pico stylesheet is minified, which looks alarming in the inspector and is how a production stylesheet is shipped. The #status region is empty when the page loads, which is correct for a region that announces later changes.

title: 4  Auditing and fixing
section: 4.5 Activity 5: choose one and fix it
text:
4.5 Activity 5: choose one and fix it
You now have a set of rows, some from axe, some from your own ears and hands. Score them as Chapter 2 says and mark the ones you would fix. Choose one to fix now: the highest score that can be changed in the time you have and that has a criterion you can check it against afterwards. A finding with no criterion is still a finding, but you cannot prove you fixed it this afternoon.
Make a branch. Find the cause in the template or the stylesheet, not the symptom: hiding an element from the checker with aria-hidden makes the report go away and the problem stay. Make the smallest change that removes the cause. Then run the pass that found it again, and the axe scan again, and ./gradlew test; the template smoke test loads every template, so a broken tag fails the build. If axe still reports the issue after your change, reload with the cache bypassed (Ctrl-Shift-R), because the stylesheet is cached and the templates are not. Take the before and after evidence as Appendix J says, and commit with a message that names the backlog row and the criterion.
The week-07-lab2-fixed tag is the state after every seeded defect is fixed, and git diff week-07-lab2-audit week-07-lab2-fixed is our fix. Read it only after your own fix is committed. Anything it changes that you did not find is a row to add to the backlog, with evidence set to reference diff, and the pass that should have caught it is the one to practise.

title: 5  Partials and pagination
text:
5.1 Activity 1: the page in parts
By the end the list is built from partials, paginated and filterable, and each of those views has a URL that works without JavaScript.
Before you start, commit your work and check out week-08. If Page is unresolved when you build, you are not on it. Keep Appendix C open for the include syntax, and give the list something to page through: with the server running, add fifteen tasks from a second terminal.
A list of a dozen tasks is fine as one page. A list of a hundred is not: a person using a screen reader walks it row by row, and everyone scrolls. A filter and pages cut the list down, and both have to produce a URL, because a view you cannot bookmark, share or reach with JavaScript off is a view that exists only while the script is running.
The row template _item.peb is unchanged in shape from Chapter 3; what is new is that the list around it is now two more partials. _list.peb renders one page of rows.
The <ul> is described by the paragraph after it, so a screen reader that lands on the list hears how many rows it holds and whether a filter is on. The empty case is a sentence in that paragraph rather than a fake row. _pager.peb renders the page controls, and renders nothing when there is one page.
Each link carries two sets of attributes again: an href with the query and the page number for the browser, and an hx-get with the same URL for HTMX. aria-current="page" marks the current position. The query is passed through urlencode because it goes into a URL, not into text.
index.peb puts the filter form above them and wraps list and pager in one element.
The filter is a GET form with a visible button, which is the whole of its no-JavaScript behaviour. hx-trigger adds the typing: input changed delay:300ms from:#filter-input fires after a pause in typing and only when the value has changed, and submit keeps the button working with the script on. #task-area is the target every list request swaps into, and hx-history-elt tells HTMX this is the element to save and restore when the back button returns to a pushed URL.
One source for the row markup is what makes the two modes stay equal. _item.peb is included by _list.peb, and _list.peb is rendered both into the page and as the fragment, so a change to a button's label or an aria-describedby lands in both modes at once. The 2025 version of this application had a separate fragment route with its own copy of the list markup, and the copies drifted.

text:
5.3 Activity 3: the pushed URL is a real URL
Type a few letters into the filter and wait. The list changes without a reload, the status box says how many tasks match, and the address bar now reads /tasks?q= and what you typed. That is hx-push-url="true": HTMX pushes the URL it requested into the browser history. Press Next and the address bar reads page=2 as well.
Now press the browser's reload button. You get the whole page, with the filter field filled in and page 2 showing. That works only because GET /tasks?q=...&page=2 answers a plain request with the full page and an HTMX request with the fragment: the same URL, two answers, told apart by the header. The 2025 version of this code fetched its fragments from a separate /tasks/fragment route, so the URL HTMX pushed was that one, and reloading it showed a bare list with no layout. One URL for both answers is what makes the pushed URL real.
Press Back. HTMX restores the saved #task-area from its history cache; when the cache has nothing, it requests the URL again with HX-History-Restore-Request: true, and isHtmxRequest() in Chapter 1 treats that as a request for the whole page. Copy the URL into a new tab, and it opens the same view.
Check the mechanics in the Network tab. A filter request shows HX-Request: true among the request headers and Vary: HX-Request among the response headers, and its response is a <ul> followed by a <nav> and the status <div>, with no <html>. If a request goes out on every keystroke, the delay or changed modifier is missing from hx-trigger. If typing sends nothing and only the button works, from:#filter-input names an id that is not on the field. If the status says that zero tasks match after you clear the field, the handler is announcing a count for an empty query.
Then switch JavaScript off (Chapter 6 has the click paths) and do the same: type, press Filter, and the page reloads with ?q= in the address bar; Previous and Next are links and reload the page; Edit on page 2 of a filtered list and Save brings you back to page 2 of that list, because the hidden fields carried the place through the redirect. The footer says which mode you are in.

title: 6  Parity and validation
text:
6.1 Activity 1: the rules in one place
By the end every route validates its input on the server, every HTMX interaction has a full-page equivalent, and you have checked both paths and written down the trade-offs.
Before you start, finish Chapter 5 on the week-08 tag, have two browsers to hand (Chrome or Edge, and Firefox), and open your backlog.
Validation lives on the server because the server is the only place both paths pass through. A browser's required attribute would stop a blank title before the server saw it, in both modes, and you would never see the server's error path, which is the one a person gets when the attribute is missing, the browser is old, or a script posts directly. The title fields in this application carry no required on purpose. Adding it is an enhancement to consider after the pilots in Chapter 8, not a default.
The two limits are constants. The messages are built from them, so a message cannot name a different number from the one the check uses. validate returns a code and a message; the code is what travels in a redirect and what the metrics in Chapter 7 record, and messageFor turns a code read back from a URL into its message, or nothing. The limits are also passed into every form's context as minTitleLength and maxTitleLength, and the hint under each field reads them. No template in the application states a number.
The 2025 version had a hint that said one limit while the check enforced another, and participants in the pilots found it by typing a title that the hint allowed and the server refused. The fix was to remove every number from the templates, not to correct one.

title: 6  Parity and validation
section: 6.5 Activity 5: what the two paths cost
text:
6.5 Activity 5: what the two paths cost
Here is what having both paths costs.
Every handler has two branches, and every behaviour has two tests. A change made in one branch and not the other is the most common defect in this codebase, and nothing but the tests catches it.
The two modes do not behave identically and cannot. Delete asks for confirmation only with the script on. The status announcement exists only with the script on: the plain path reloads and says nothing, which is the backlog row you wrote in Chapter 1. After a swap, focus is where the markup puts it; after a reload, the page scrolls to the top first.
The status codes are not the whole truth. A failed validation is 200 in one mode and 303 in the other, so anything that counts failures by status counts wrong.
State travels in URLs. A failed submission redirects with the typed title in the query string, which lands in the browser history and the server log. A title is the person's own text, and Appendix F is about why that matters.
The markup is longer. Every form carries hidden q and page fields, every link carries them in its query string, and every control carries both a plain attribute and an hx- one.
One URL with two answers needs Vary. A cache that ignores it serves a fragment as a page.
The plain path is slower per action. Every action is a whole page, not a few lines of it, and on a slow connection that is the difference between a pause and a wait.
The hx- attributes and the header check are a second vocabulary on top of HTML and HTTP; Appendix D exists because of it.
What the two paths buy is a page that works when the script does not load, is blocked or is off, and one piece of HTML for the browser and the screen reader alike. The GOV.UK service manual requires it for services the public has no choice but to use (Government Digital Service, no date a). We think the costs above are worth paying for an application like this one. For a drawing tool or a game they would not be, and saying so is part of the trade-off.

title: 7  Instrumentation
text:
7.1 Measuring rather than asking
By the end you have an evaluation plan that names three to five tasks, each with a code, a success criterion and a definition of error, and you have watched the reference code write one metrics row per request in both modes and label those rows with a participant code.
Before you start, check out the week-09 tag and run ./gradlew build; if timed is unresolved anywhere, you are on an earlier tag. Have research/stories.md and backlog/backlog.csv from Chapter 2 open. Read the metric definitions in Appendix I once; this chapter uses them without restating them.
This chapter and the next find out what happens when people use the prototype, by measuring. The measurement comes from the server: every request the application handles writes one row to a metrics file. Nothing else is involved: no analytics script in the page, no third party, and nothing about the person beyond the pseudonym in the session column, which they can ask to have deleted. That log is a narrow instrument. It sees that a request arrived, what it was for, whether it succeeded, how long the server took, and when. It does not see the participant read the screen, hesitate, look for a button, or say "did that work?". Those come from the person sitting next to the participant with a notebook, which is Chapter 8; the two halves are put together in Chapter 9.

title: 7  Instrumentation
text:
7.2 Activity 1: write the evaluation plan
Create research/plan.md. It has three parts: the tasks, the measures, and the design of the sessions.
A task is something a participant is asked to do with the task list, written as a scenario you can read aloud: "You have been asked to find every task about the quarterly report. Use the filter and tell me how many there are." Each task carries one of the codes in utils/TaskCodes.kt, because the metrics file records the code and nothing else about the task, so the plan has to be the place that says what T1_filter meant. Choose three to five of the five participant tasks: filter, edit, add, delete and mark done. T0_list is the page load and the redirects that follow a change without JavaScript, not a task anyone is asked to do.


src/main/kotlin/utils/TaskCodes.kt

package utils

/**
 * Codes for the tasks participants carry out in the Week 9 evaluation. They are the
 * task_code column of the metrics and are stated nowhere else.
 */
object TaskCodes {
    const val LIST = "T0_list"
    const val FILTER = "T1_filter"
    const val EDIT = "T2_edit"
    const val ADD = "T3_add"
    const val DELETE = "T4_delete"
    const val TOGGLE = "T5_toggle"

    val all = listOf(LIST, FILTER, EDIT, ADD, DELETE, TOGGLE)
}

For each task write the success criterion as something the facilitator can see or hear: the participant says "three", the new title is in the list, the task is gone. Then write what counts as an error. The log counts one kind of error on its own, a submission the server rejected, which it records as a validation_error row with the reason in the outcome column. Everything else, such as deleting the wrong task, succeeds as far as the server is concerned and is an error only if the note-taker writes it down. Say in the plan which errors you expect from the log and which from the notes, so that in Chapter 9 you are not tempted to add the two together.
Write the tasks against seed data you control. Decide the ten or so titles the list will hold at the start of every session, so that a scenario can name "Submit invoices" and the participant can find it; Activity 4 shows how to save them. Put delete last, because it is the destructive one, and give each task a time after which the facilitator moves on; two minutes is enough for any of these.
The measures section says which metrics you will report and names Appendix I as the definition of each. The design section is short: four participants, every participant does the tasks in both modes, two start with HTMX and two without JavaScript, and the comparison is within each participant. Chapter 8 explains why, and what that design can and cannot support; the plan only has to record it.

7  Instrumentation
text:
7.4 Activity 3: label a participant's session
The first time a browser visits the application the server sets a sid cookie to six random hex characters, and every row that browser produces carries them. Before a pilot session you replace that value with the participant's pseudonym, so that the rows can be told apart later and deleted on request. The cookie is readable from JavaScript on purpose. Open the browser console on a tab showing the application, type document.cookie = "sid=P1; path=/" with the participant's code in place of P1, and reload the page.
The check is the page footer, which shows the mode and the session code the next row will carry; the route tests at this tag assert both that the footer shows a sent code and that the row does. If the footer still shows six hex characters, the cookie was set in a console belonging to a different tab, or the page was not reloaded. A cookie set from /tasks without path=/ is still honoured, because the browser defaults the path to /, so that is not the cause. If the footer shows the previous participant's code, you have not changed it, and two people's rows will merge under one pseudonym, which cannot be undone afterwards.

Then turn JavaScript off and do it again. In Firefox set javascript.enabled to false in about:config. Reload after the change and look at the footer: it says "no JavaScript" when the script did not run and "HTMX" when it did.
Open data/metrics.csv. Expect one row for each thing you did, plus one T0_list row after each change without JavaScript, written about a second later by the GET the redirect caused. The excerpt below, from the example data in the week-10 tag, shows a rejected add followed by a successful one in that mode, each followed by its redirect; the header is the one in the comment on LogEntry. title: 8  Pilots
text:
8.1 What four people can tell you
By the end you have run four pilot sessions with consenting participants, each in both modes, and you have a metrics file and a set of notes that Chapter 9 can work from.
Before you start, you need the plan and seed data from Chapter 7 and a dry run that passed; the participant information sheet from Appendix G and the consent form from Appendix H, copied into research/ with the blanks filled from your institution's page; and four people from outside your pair who have agreed to give you twenty minutes each.
Every participant does the same tasks twice, once with HTMX and once with JavaScript off, and the comparison is between a person's two passes rather than between two groups of people. This is a within-subject design. It uses each participant twice, which with four of them matters, and it removes the largest source of noise, that people differ from each other far more than the two modes do. It brings one problem of its own: the second pass is always easier, because the participant has just done the tasks. Counterbalancing halves that problem. P1 and P3 start with HTMX, P2 and P4 start without JavaScript, so that each mode is first for two people. It does not remove it, and with two people per order you cannot separate the order effect from the mode effect; say so when you report.
What the design supports is a descriptive comparison: for each participant, the time on task and the errors in each mode, side by side, and then how many of the four were faster or made fewer errors in which mode and by how much. It supports the observation that a failure happened in front of you, which is enough to put it on the backlog. It does not support a claim about people in general, and it does not support a hypothesis test; with four participants a p-value is theatre, and this book does not compute one. Appendix I says how to write the comparison up.

title: 8  Pilots
text:
8.2 Activity 1: prepare the room
Start the server, copy research/seed-tasks.csv to data/tasks.csv, and delete data/metrics.csv if it holds anything from the dry run; the first request writes a fresh file. Have the application open in a browser with no other tabs, DevTools closed, and the bookmarks bar hidden. Work in pairs: one of you facilitates and one takes notes, and you swap between sessions. Have research/plan.md open where the facilitator can read from it and a file research/pilots/P1.md open where the note-taker can type.
Start research/consent-log.md with one line per participant: pseudonym, date, which mode they did first, and that consent was given. Nothing else about them goes in it.

title: 8  Pilots
text:
8.3 Activity 2: run a session
Hand the participant the information sheet and give them time to read it. Then the facilitator says, in their own words, something of this length:
"Thanks for doing this. We are testing the task list, not you, so there is nothing you can get wrong. I will read you a few short tasks and you do them; I will not help, but you can stop at any point. The server records what it does, under the code P1 rather than your name, and my partner is taking notes. Nothing is recorded or filmed. Are you happy to go ahead?"
The participant initials the consent form, you write the pseudonym and the date on it, and the form goes in the folder, not in the repository. Set the sid cookie to the pseudonym as in Chapter 7 and check that the footer shows it. Set the mode for the first pass the way the same chapter describes, and check the footer again.
Give the participant a minute with the list before the first task, untimed. Then, for each task, read the scenario from the plan once, and watch. The note-taker writes the time the scenario was read, what the participant did first, every hesitation of more than a few seconds and what they were looking at during it, anything they said, word for word where you can, whether they noticed the status message or the redirected page, and whether the task was completed, not completed, or completed after help. When the participant says they have finished, or the time limit passes, ask one question: "On a scale of one to five, how confident are you that that worked?" Write the number down with the task code. Then the next task.
Do not help. If the participant is stuck, let them be stuck; where they look and what they try is the finding. After about two minutes, ask "what are you looking for?", which tells you what they expected without telling them where it is. If they are still stuck, say "let's move to the next task" and record the task as not completed, with the reason. If they are frustrated rather than stuck, offer to stop. A participant who wants to leave, leaves, and their rows stay in the log unless they ask for them to go.
Between the passes, switch the mode, reload, check the footer, and tell the participant that the page will now work slightly differently. Run the same tasks in the same order. The second pass is faster for everyone; that is the order effect, and it is why half your participants did this pass first.

title: 8  Pilots
text:
8.4 Activity 3: debrief
Ask three questions and write the answers down as said: which task was hardest and why; whether anything surprised them or did not do what they expected; and whether there was a moment when they were not sure something had worked. If they used the keyboard alone or a screen reader, ask whether anything was unreachable. Do not explain the design or defend it; if they ask why something works the way it does, say you will tell them after the last session. Thank them, remind them that they can ask for their rows to be deleted by quoting the pseudonym, and show them where that is written on the information sheet.

title: 8  Pilots
section: 8.5 Activity 4: check the log before they leave
text:
8.5 Activity 4: check the log before they leave
While the participant is still there, open data/metrics.csv and look at the rows for their pseudonym. There should be rows in both modes, the number of validation_error rows should match the errors the note-taker saw, and every task in the plan should have the row the plan said would mark its end. If a task has no row, do not ask the participant to repeat it; a repeat would be a third pass and not the same measurement. Note what is missing in research/pilots/P1.md and keep the note-taker's record of that task instead. If the rows carry six hex characters instead of the pseudonym, the cookie was never set; the timestamps will still let you attribute them, so write the start and end times of the session in the notes now and set the cookie for the next person before they sit down.
Reset for the next participant: copy the seed tasks back, set the cookie to the next pseudonym, set the mode for their first pass.

title: 8  Pilots
text:
8.6 What to record
When the fourth session is done, copy data/metrics.csv to research/metrics.csv and commit it with research/pilots/P1.md to P4.md and research/consent-log.md. The metrics file holds pseudonyms and timings and nothing else, and Appendix F says why that can go in the repository when the consent forms cannot. Read the notes for names before committing; a participant who said "I'd do it the way Sam does" has named someone, and the name comes out.
Write one paragraph at the end of each participant's notes on what went wrong procedurally: a cookie set late, a task read twice, a server restarted. Chapter 9 reads those paragraphs before it reads the numbers.

Nielsen's argument for five participants in a formative test is the source of the small-sample tradition this chapter sits in, and worth reading for what it does and does not claim (Nielsen, 2012). The W3C's page on involving people with disabilities in evaluation is short and says what to do when a participant uses assistive technology (W3C Web Accessibility Initiative, 2021).

title: 9  Analysis and prioritisation
text:
9.1 Two kinds of bug
By the end you have a findings file that turns four participants' metrics and notes into ranked findings, each with the rows and lines behind it, and a backlog whose top row is the change you make in Chapter 10.
Before you start, check out the week-10 tag and run ./gradlew build; it now compiles tools/ as well, and ./gradlew tasks --group evaluation lists analyse. Have research/metrics.csv, research/pilots/P1.md to P4.md and research/plan.md from Chapter 8 open, and Appendix I to hand; this chapter uses its definitions without restating them.
How do we know the task list works? A developer has three answers: it compiles, the tests pass, I used it and it worked for me. None of them says how anyone else fared. The audit in Chapter 4 found the first kind of bug, the kind you can see: a field with no label, a link with no text. The pilots recorded the second kind, the kind you can only measure. A participant without JavaScript who submitted a two-letter title saw the page reload and nothing else, because the status region is empty after a redirect, and said nothing about it at the debrief, because from where they sat nothing had happened. The server wrote a validation_error row at the second it happened. This chapter is where rows like that become findings, and where the notes say what the rows cannot.

title: 9  Analysis and prioritisation
section: 9.2 Activity 1: read the notes before the numbers
text:
9.2 Activity 1: read the notes before the numbers
Open the four notes files and read the procedural paragraph at the end of each one first. A cookie set late, a server restarted, a task read twice: each changes what that participant's rows mean, and the decision about them is made now, before any number is computed, so that the numbers cannot influence it. Start research/findings.md with a section called Data and write one line per participant: the pseudonym, the order of the modes, and any rows excluded or re-attributed and why. Rows under six hex characters that belong to a participant whose cookie was set late are re-attributed by timestamp, as Chapter 8 said; write the time range you used.
Count the rows per pseudonym and mode in research/metrics.csv and write the counts in the same section. A participant with rows in only one mode contributes nothing to the comparison between modes; they still contribute notes.

title: 9  Analysis and prioritisation
section: 9.3 Activity 2: run the tool and read its table
text:
9.3 Activity 2: run the tool and read its table
Run the tool on the example file at this tag first, so that you know what the table looks like when it is right:
./gradlew analyse -Pfile=data/example-metrics.csv

The tool groups the rows by task code and mode and prints one line per group. n_success and errors are counts of rows, error_rate is errors over their sum, and the median and MAD are of the successful requests only; summarise is where that is decided:


tools/Analyse.kt

/** One summary per task code and js_mode, sorted. Median and MAD use the successful requests only. */
fun summarise(rows: List<MetricRow>): List<Summary> =
    rows.groupBy { it.taskCode to it.jsMode }
        .toSortedMap(compareBy({ it.first }, { it.second }))
        .map { (key, group) ->
            val successMs = group.filter { it.step == "success" }.map { it.ms }
            Summary(key.first, key.second, successMs.size, median(successMs), mad(successMs), group.size - successMs.size)
        }

median_ms and mad_ms are server time. In the example they lie between 10 and 48 milliseconds, and the gap between the modes is the cost of rendering a page rather than a fragment. They say nothing about participants; the one question they answer is whether a change slowed the server, which is Chapter 10's question. Error rate is the column that carries a finding: in the example, the edit task failed in two of six requests without JavaScript and two of eight with it, adding failed in two of six and one of seven, and nothing else failed.
Two things about the rows come from driving a browser against this code, and both change how you read the edit line. Without JavaScript every action writes two rows, the POST that answers 303 and the list GET the browser makes next, which is why T0_list has sixteen successes in the plain mode and three with HTMX; it is not a task, and its line only confirms that the redirects happened. And opening the edit form writes a T2_edit row in both modes: HTMX fetches the form as a fragment, and without JavaScript the Edit button loads the list with one row as a form, which the list route logs under the edit code. So for every edit there is one opening row and then one row per save, and the denominator for the edit error rate is the number of saves, which the tool does not know. For the example data that is two errors in five saves with HTMX and two in four without, not two in eight requests and two in six. Find the saves from the timestamps, write the denominator in the finding, and say that the tool's figure is per request.
Now run ./gradlew analyse -Pfile=research/metrics.csv and read your own table the same way. If the tool stops with a message that a column is missing, the file was edited in a spreadsheet that renamed the header; take the copy from data/ again.

title: 9  Analysis and prioritisation
section: 9.4 Activity 3: time on task from the timestamps
text:
9.4 Activity 3: time on task from the timestamps
The tool does not compute time on task, because which row ends a task is a judgement your plan made. Open research/metrics.csv in a spreadsheet, sort by session_id and then ts_iso, and for each participant, mode and task find the row your plan named as the end of that task and the row before it; the gap in seconds is the time on task as Appendix I defines it, a few seconds high for everyone in the same way. For four participants, five tasks and two modes that is forty numbers, an hour's careful work, and not worth automating for one study. Put them in a table in findings.md with a row per participant and a column per task and mode. The example data cannot be used for this, since each of its participants did one mode only.
Under each task, compute the median and MAD across the four participants in each mode, and for each participant the difference between their two modes. Then write the sentence Appendix I asks for: how many of the four were faster in which mode and by how much, naming anyone who went the other way. If two differences are a few seconds and two are a minute, you have two findings, not an average.

title: 9  Analysis and prioritisation
section: 9.5 Activity 4: join the numbers to the notes
text:
9.5 Activity 4: join the numbers to the notes
Read the notes for what they say about each task, and write one finding per thing the data and the notes agree happened. A finding is a paragraph with a short heading carrying three things: what the numbers say, with the rows behind them (the file, the pseudonym and the timestamps, so that a reader can find them); what the notes say, with the file and line, quoting the participant where there is a quote; and who it falls on, which is the inclusion column of your backlog. An illustrative finding, not from any pilot: "P2 and P4, both without JavaScript, submitted a blank title on their second edit (metrics.csv, P2 at 14:21:03 and 14:21:30, P4 at 15:02:11). P2 said 'I thought it had saved' (P2.md line 23). Falls on anyone using the plain path, which includes people on locked-down machines and some screen reader configurations." The confidence scores and the completion counts go in the finding for the task they belong to, and low confidence after a completed task is a finding about feedback in its own right.
Findings the log cannot see go in too: a participant who deleted the wrong task, a participant who never found Edit. Their denominators come from the notes, and they are not added to the logged errors, as Appendix I says.
Three findings is the minimum, each with a source a reader can open. A claim with no row and no line behind it is an impression, and goes in a section called Impressions, where nobody can mistake it for a finding.

title: 9  Analysis and prioritisation
text:
9.6 Activity 5: prioritise against cost
Each finding becomes a backlog row, or updates a row the audit or the interviews already created, with evidence pointing at research/findings.md and the heading. Score the rows as Chapter 2 says. Then add what you could not add before you had measured anything: what a fix would cost, in files touched and in the checks it needs afterwards. A change to a template and its test is an afternoon. A change to the routes or the storage is a day, plus the parity table from Chapter 6 run again.
Rank the rows, highest score first and, within a score, lowest cost first. The top row is the change you make in Chapter 10. Under the ranking write one sentence for every row you are not fixing and why; a finding with a high score that needs a day stays on the backlog with that reason, and the reason is read by whoever picks the project up after you. A defect you could see, from the audit, and a defect you could only measure, from the pilots, sit in the same ranking. The method does not care which kind it is.

title: 9  Analysis and prioritisation
text:
9.7 What to record
Commit research/findings.md and the updated backlog/backlog.csv. The findings file holds the Data section, the time-on-task table, the tool's output as you ran it, with the command and the commit of the metrics file it read, the findings, the impressions, and the ranking with its reasons. Do not edit research/metrics.csv. If a row is excluded, the finding says so and the row stays, because the chain in Chapter 11 is only as good as the data a reader can reopen.

title: 10  Redesign and verification
text:
10.1 Smaller than the bug report
By the end you have made the top-ranked change, run the twenty regression checks on it, re-piloted with two new participants, and written the chain from finding to verification with a file behind each link.
Before you start, you need the ranking from Chapter 9, a branch made from the week-10 tag, and two participants booked who were not among the first four. Have the parity table from Chapter 6 to hand.
The change is one change, and it is small. The finding named a task, a mode and a cause; the change removes the cause and nothing else. A few files and thirty lines is the shape of most fixes to this application, and a fix that touches ten files is either two fixes or a redesign the evidence did not ask for.
For a validation finding, three layers are available, and they catch different people. A browser attribute such as minlength stops the submission before it leaves the page, for anyone whose browser honours it. A CSS rule on :user-invalid shows the field in its error state as soon as the person leaves it, for anyone who can see it. The server, which already marks the field with aria-invalid and links the message with aria-describedby, catches what the other two miss, a script, an old browser, a form posted from elsewhere, and is the layer a screen reader hears. Chapter 6 left required and minlength off on purpose so that the server's path was the one you measured; this is the point where you decide, from your own data, whether to add them.
If you do, know what it does to your instrument. A submission the browser blocks never reaches the server, so after the change the validation_error rows for that task fall to zero whether or not people stopped making the mistake. The log has gone blind to the attempt, and a zero in the after table is the fix and the blind spot together. The note-taker counts browser-blocked submissions in the re-pilot, and the write-up gives that count beside the zero.

title: 10  Redesign and verification
section: 10.2 Activity 1: write the change down first
text:
10.2 Activity 1: write the change down first
Under the top finding in research/findings.md, add a section headed Change, written before you open an editor. It names the files that will change; what a participant will see differently in each mode, one sentence each; which number in the before table should move and in which direction; which numbers should not move, always including the median server time and the parity rows for the routes you touch; and the WCAG criterion to check against, if the finding named one. This is the acceptance criterion, written now so that the result cannot rewrite it.

title: 10  Redesign and verification
text:
10.3 Activity 2: make it
Make the smallest change that removes the cause, in both modes, on your branch. Run ./gradlew test: the template smoke test loads every template and the route tests exercise every route in both modes, so a change that breaks either fails here and not in front of a participant. Then start the server and do the changed task yourself in both modes, switching as Chapter 7 showed, and read the footer to know which mode you are in.
Three things catch people here. A changed stylesheet is cached and a changed template is not, so a CSS change that does not appear needs a reload with the cache bypassed (Ctrl-Shift-R). HTMX does not swap a 4xx response by default, so a change that sends 400 on a validation error makes the error vanish with JavaScript on; Chapter 7 said why the routes answer 200 and 303. And a fragment given autofocus moves focus to that control every time it is swapped in, which is what you want for an error and not for a status message.
Commit on the branch with a message that names the finding's heading and the criterion. The commit hash is the third link in the chain.

title: 10  Redesign and verification
section: 10.5 Activity 4: re-pilot with two new participants
text:
10.5 Activity 4: re-pilot with two new participants
The first four participants have done the tasks twice and know where everything is; a third pass from them measures their memory. Recruit two people who have not seen the list and run the procedure from Chapter 8 unchanged: the same plan and seed data, pseudonyms P5 and P6, one starting in each mode, on your branch, with the metrics file deleted first. If your change moved a check into the browser, the note-taker tallies each time the browser refused a submission, next to the task code. Copy the metrics file to research/metrics-after.csv and the notes to research/pilots/P5.md and P6.md, read both for names, and commit.

title: 10  Redesign and verification
10  Redesign and verification
text:
10.7 What to record
The chain has four links and a file behind each: the finding (research/findings.md, the heading), the measurement (research/metrics.csv, the rows, and the before table), the change (the commit hash and git diff against the tag), and the verification (research/regression.csv, research/metrics-after.csv, the after table and the two participants' notes). Merge the branch, tag the result with a name of your own, and write the tag in the findings file; Chapter 11 presents the chain and Chapter 12 links to it.

title: 10  Redesign and verification
text:
10.8 Further reading
GOV.UK's error summary pattern is the published design for telling a person what went wrong with a form, and the reference code's summary follows it (Government Digital Service, no date). Deque's account of how much of WCAG an automated checker can find is the reason most rows of the regression table are run by a person (Deque Systems, 2021).

title: 11  Crit
text:
11.1 What a crit is for
By the end you have presented one evidence chain to a group of peers in five minutes, answered their questions from the files rather than from memory, written a response to each of theirs, and recorded the questions you could not answer.
Before the lab, finish the evidence chain from Chapter 10, have the application running at the tag that holds your fix, and bring the before and after screenshots named as Appendix J describes. Nothing in this chapter changes the code.
A crit is a conversation about one piece of work with the evidence in the room. You put the chain in front of people who were not there when you built it, and they find the step that only holds together because you remember it doing so. That step is worth finding now, while there is a week to fix it, rather than when the marker reaches it.
The chain has four links, and you present them in order: the finding, the measurement that showed it, the fix, and the verification that the fix worked. Each link has a file behind it. The finding is a backlog row and the notes it points at; the measurement is rows of the metrics file and the figures Chapter 9 computed from them; the fix is a commit; the verification is the regression checklist and the re-pilot from Chapter 10. If one link has no file, you have found the gap before anyone else does.
The audience responds to the evidence, not the person. "The focus ring is faint" is about the work; "you did not test it properly" is about you, and the second kind is not permitted here. The useful question asks to see something: which rows of the metrics file, which line of the notes, what the no-JS path did at the same point, what the screen reader said. A question that cannot be answered from a file is still useful, because it tells the presenter what the portfolio is missing.

title: 11  Crit
text:
11.2 Activity 1: prepare the chain
Choose the chain you will present. If you fixed more than one thing, choose the fix with the strongest measurement behind it, not the one you are proudest of. Write crit/outline.md with four headings, finding, measurement, fix and verification, and under each the sentence you will say and the path of the file you will show. The sentence names the thing and the figure: "participants without JavaScript failed the edit task in two of six attempts", not "the edit task had problems". Keep the file under a page; it is a prompt sheet, not a script.
Decide what you will show live and what you will show as a screenshot. Showing the fixed behaviour live is stronger than a picture of it, because the picture could be from any commit. Showing the broken behaviour live means checking out the earlier tag during your five minutes, which is time you do not have; the before screenshot carries that link. If you will demonstrate with a screen reader, test the volume in the room before your turn, and say what it announces as it announces it, because the people at the back will not hear it.
Three things go wrong at this point. The server is not running when your turn comes, because somebody stopped it to run their own; start yours before the session and leave that terminal alone. JavaScript is still off in the browser from your last parity check, so the HTMX path looks broken; check once before you begin. A screenshot that would have carried a link is on a laptop at home; the fallback for every live step is a file already in the repository.

title: 11  Crit
text:
11.3 Activity 2: the crit
Work in groups of five or six. Each person has twelve minutes: five to present, five for questions and answers, two for the group to write. One person keeps time and says "two minutes" and "stop"; the session fails when the first presenter takes twenty. Agree the order at the start so nobody is surprised.
As the presenter, say the four sentences from your outline in order, showing the file or the behaviour behind each. Narrate what is not visible: "I am pressing Tab; focus is on the Edit button; I press Enter". When you have said the fourth sentence, stop, even with time left. Five minutes is enough for one chain and not enough for two.
As a questioner, ask for what you could not see. If the measurement was a rate, ask what the denominator was. If the fix was shown with JavaScript on, ask what the no-JS path does at the same point. If a screenshot stood in for a live step, ask which commit it came from. If you think the fix might have broken something else, ask which regression check covers it. One question each, then a second round if there is time.
As the presenter during questions, answer from the evidence or say that you cannot. "That is rows 41 to 46" is an answer; "I think it was about a third" is not; "I did not record that" is an honest answer you will act on in Activity 4. Do not argue. A question you disagree with is still a question a marker could ask, and the written response is where you say why the evidence does not support the concern.

title: 11  Crit
text:
11.4 Activity 3: the written response
In the last two minutes of each turn, every listener writes three sentences for the presenter: what they saw, what they could not see, and one question they would put to the portfolio. "What they saw" names a link in the chain and the file that carried it. "What they could not see" names a link that was asserted rather than shown. The question is one a reader of the portfolio could reasonably ask. Hand the sheet over or paste the text into the presenter's shared file. Do not put your name on it: it is going into a repository that must contain no names (Chapter 12).
An illustrative example of the three sentences, not a response anyone gave: "I saw the before and after error rates for the edit task and the metrics rows they came from. I did not see the regression check that covers deleting a task now that the edit form has changed. Does the no-JS edit path keep the typed title when validation fails?"
Keep the responses you receive in crit/responses.md, one block per response, as given. Do not tidy or summarise them; the gaps they name are the evidence that you looked for gaps.

title: 11  Crit
text:
11.5 Activity 4: what the presenter records
After your turn, while you still remember the room, write crit/notes.md. For each question you were asked, record the question, what you answered at the time, and what you will do about it. There are three kinds of action. The evidence exists and the portfolio did not point at it: add the link. The evidence does not exist and can be gathered in the time left: gather it, and the note says where it will go. The evidence does not exist and cannot be gathered: write the limitation in a sentence, which goes into the portfolio as something stated rather than something a reader discovers. A question that leads to new work is a new backlog row, with its evidence column pointing at crit/notes.md.
The questions you could not answer are the most useful output of the day. They go to Chapter 12, where each becomes a link, a new file, or a stated limitation.

title: 11  Crit
text:
11.6 What to record
Commit crit/outline.md, crit/responses.md and crit/notes.md. Check that none of the three contains a name, a student number or an email address. Recording the session on video or audio is not part of this chapter; if your group wants to, everyone in the room consents first, and the recording stays out of the repository.

title: 12  Portfolio
text:
12.1 What the portfolio is
By the end you have a README in which every claim links to the data, code or screenshot that supports it, a reflection of two paragraphs, and a tag that a stranger can clone, build and read.
Before the lab, read crit/notes.md from Chapter 11 and have the assessment page open, because it holds the pass criteria this chapter builds towards and nothing here restates them. You need about two hours and no new code.
The portfolio is the README of your repository and the files it points at. It is not a separate document, a slide deck or a folder of screenshots; it is the front page of the work, written for a reader who was not there and has little time. That reader opens the README at the tag you name, follows the links, and decides whether each claim is supported by what they find at the other end. A claim with no link is an assertion, and the assessment treats it as one.
Every file the README points at already exists if you have followed the chapters in order: the consent record, notes, stories and backlog from Chapter 2; the audit record and fix from Chapter 4; the metrics file from Chapter 7; the pilot notes from Chapter 8; the analysis from Chapter 9; the regression checklist and re-pilot from Chapter 10; the screenshots named as Appendix J says; and the three crit files. This chapter adds the README and a tag. If a link you want to write has nothing to point at, the portfolio has found a gap, and the honest response is a sentence saying so, not a link to the nearest thing.

title: 12  Portfolio
text:
12.2 Activity 1: act on the crit
Open crit/notes.md. For each question, do what the note says: add the link, gather the evidence, or write the limitation. Where the evidence exists, the link is written in Activity 2. Where it can still be gathered, gather it now and commit it before you write a word of the README, because a link to an uncommitted file breaks at the tag. Where it cannot be gathered, write the sentence that states the limitation and keep it for the limitations section.
Re-running a pilot is not expected unless the crit found a flaw in the method, such as a participant who was told the answer. Polish the record; do not rerun the study.

title: 12  Portfolio
text:
12.3 Activity 2: write the README
Write the README in this order. Each section is a few sentences and the links that support them, and the whole file fits on two screens.
The first section says what the application is in two sentences and how to run it, by pointing at Appendix A rather than repeating its commands. It names the tag the portfolio describes, so the reader knows which commit the links resolve against.
The second section says how many participants took part in the pilots and in the re-pilot, in which modes, and that consent was recorded, with a link to the consent record. No names, no student numbers, no email addresses, nothing a participant could be recognised from; participants appear only by the codes Chapter 8 assigned.
The third section lists the findings, one sentence each, with a link after every sentence to the rows or lines that support it. A finding is a claim about what happened: "participants without JavaScript failed the edit task in two of four saves", followed by a link to those rows of the metrics file and to the line of the notes where a participant said why. The example data at the week-10 tag, read as Chapter 9 and Chapter 10 read it, shows the shape at paragraph length. A finding with an accessibility cause names its success criterion by number (W3C, 2023).
The fourth section lists the fixes, one to three, each with the finding it addresses, the criterion it serves, and a link to the commit or the diff. A fix that did not move its measurement is still a fix; say what the measurement did and what you make of it.
The fifth section is the verification: a link to the completed regression checklist, a link to the re-pilot data, and the before and after figures side by side with their sources. A regression check that failed and was not fixed is said here, not left as a blank row.
The sixth section is limitations: what you did not do, what the sample size does not support, and the questions from the crit you could not answer. One paragraph. A limitation stated here is professional practice; the same limitation discovered by the reader is a gap.
The seventh section is the reflection from Activity 3.
Links are relative paths within the repository, with a line or row where one applies, in the form the forge turns into a link to those lines (#L41-L46 after a file path works on GitHub and GitLab). A reader who has cloned the repository opens the same path. Links to your working copy, to a cloud drive or to a chat message resolve for nobody else.

title: 12  Portfolio
text:
12.4 Activity 3: the reflection
Write two paragraphs of prose at the end of the README, with no headings, bullets or template. The first paragraph is about the evidence: where the chain from finding to verification was strongest, where it was weakest, and which question from the crit you could not answer. The second is about what comes next: what you would measure that you did not, who you would recruit, and which backlog row you would take on, with the row named. A reader should be able to check each sentence against a file in the repository, the same as the rest of the README.
Two things make a reflection worthless. A set of headings with one sentence under each, "what went well" and "what was challenging", says nothing a reader can act on; write sentences that connect. Praise for your own work does not belong in it; the evidence is in the sections above, and the reflection is for what the evidence does not show.

title: 12  Portfolio
text:
12.5 Activity 4: check, tag, submit
Three checks, in order, before you tag.
No personal data anywhere. Search the working tree for email addresses with git grep -n -i -E '[a-z0-9._-]+@[a-z0-9.-]+\.[a-z]+'; the only hit should be your own address, if that. Search the history for each participant's real name with git log -p -S'<name>'; a name in an old commit is still in the repository even after the file was changed. Open every screenshot and look at the browser tabs, the bookmark bar and the window title. If a name is in the history, deleting the file does not remove it; tell the module team before you tag, because the fix rewrites history and is not yours to do alone.
Every link resolves. Open the README on the forge's web view at the commit you are about to tag and click every link. A link that works in your editor and not on the web view points at a file that was never committed. The metrics file is the usual one: the reference repository ignores data/*.csv apart from the example files, so a link to the pilot data breaks at the tag unless the data was copied into a committed location when the pilots ended. If it was not, copy it now, commit the copy, and point the links at it.

git clone <your repository address> check
cd check
git checkout <the commit you will tag>
./gradlew run
Open the page as Appendix A says, add a task, stop the server with Ctrl-C and delete the clone. If the clone fails to build and your working copy does not, a file the build depends on was never committed; git status in the working copy names it.
Then tag and push:
git tag -a <tag name> -m "Portfolio"
git push origin <tag name>

14.2 What passes
A submission passes when all of the following hold.
Participants. At least two people took part in the pilots of Chapter 8, and four is the aim. At least one of them used the application in a mode other than mouse with JavaScript: keyboard only, a screen reader, or JavaScript off. Consent is recorded for each, and no participant can be identified from anything in the repository, its history or its screenshots.
Findings. At least three findings, each with a source a reader can open: rows of the metrics file, lines of the pilot notes, or both. A finding with an accessibility cause names its WCAG success criterion (W3C, 2023).
Fixes. One to three changes to the code, each with a diff, each addressing a named finding. One change done well is worth more than three half done.
Verification. At least [10 | 20] of the twenty regression checks in Chapter 10 completed, with no Level A failure remaining. At least one criterion moved from fail to pass. A re-pilot with at least one participant, two being the aim, in the mode the fix is for, with the before and after figures shown side by side. Both paths, enhanced and plain, still work.
Honesty. A change that did not improve its measurement is reported as such, with what you make of it. Limitations are stated by you, not discovered by the reader.

Fewer than two participants, no metrics file, no change to the code, or fewer than [10 | 20] regression checks completed.

14.5 What the marker does, in order
First, the marker opens the README at the named tag and checks that the files it links to exist, that the metrics file has at least two participant codes, that there are three findings, a diff and regression data, and looks for the fail triggers: data that is too clean, notes that are missing, claims that contradict the data, personal data in two or three screenshots chosen at random. Second, the marker follows the three links of each chain: from each finding to its data, from each fix to its finding, and from each fix to its verification. How many chains close sets the band.

Fourth, the marker reads the limitations and the reflection for honest reporting and checks that the plain path still works.
Last, the marker records the mark, the band, the outcome and two or three sentences of feedback naming what was strong and what was missing. This order is why the README in Chapter 12 is written in the order it is.

Address already in use: a server from last time is still running, usually in a terminal you closed without stopping it. Find and stop it, or run on another port for now with PORT=8081 ./gradlew run and open the page on that port.

B.1 Declarations
This appendix is for a reader who knows Java, Python or JavaScript and has not met Kotlin; by the end you can read every file the chapters include, and you will not have written a line.
The book's code is Kotlin on the JVM, served by Ktor and rendered by Pebble. The chapters say what each piece does; this page says what the syntax means, with the real lines from the reference code as the examples. If a construct is not here, the Kotlin documentation's basic syntax page covers it in a screen or two (JetBrains, no date a).
val declares a name that is assigned once; var declares one that can be reassigned. Almost everything in this code is a val. B.5 Data classes
