/**
 * One task. The id is a UUID string, so a task keeps its identity when the CSV file is
 * rewritten. Nothing here identifies a person.
 */
data class Task(
    val id: String = UUID.randomUUID().toString(),
    val title: String,
    val completed: Boolean = false,
    val createdAt: LocalDateTime = LocalDateTime.now(),
) {
    /** The shape templates see. Dates arrive formatted so templates do no formatting. */
    fun toPebbleContext(): Map<String, Any> =
        mapOf(
            "id" to id,
            "title" to title,
            "completed" to completed,
            "createdAt" to createdAt.format(DISPLAY_FORMAT),
            "createdAtISO" to createdAt.format(DateTimeFormatter.ISO_LOCAL_DATE_TIME),
        )

A data class is a class whose purpose is to hold values. Its constructor is in the header, each parameter with val becomes a read-only property, and defaults fill in what a caller omits, so Task(title = "Milk") is a complete task with a fresh id. The compiler writes equals, hashCode, toString and copy. Because the properties are read-only, changing a task means making a changed copy: task.copy(completed = !task.completed) in TaskStore above gives a new task with one field different and the rest the same. A method body goes in the braces after the header, as toPebbleContext does. Comments between /** */ are documentation comments, as in Java.

title: Appendix C: Pebble
text:
C.1 How the engine is set up
This appendix covers the Pebble template syntax the book uses and ends with a cheatsheet for finding one row.
Pebble is a template engine for the JVM with syntax in the Twig and Jinja family; the reference code uses version 3.2.4 (Pebble Templates, no date). A template is a text file, in this book always HTML, with expressions, tags and comments embedded in it. The server fills it from a map of values and sends the result. Every page and every fragment the application sends is a template, and nothing is built by joining strings in Kotlin, which is what keeps the escaping in one place.
Three settings matter. autoEscaping(true) escapes every { } for HTML; the raw filter turns that off for one expression, and the reference code never uses it. cacheActive(false) re-reads a template on every request, so an edit shows on the next reload without a restart; a deployed application would turn the cache on. strictVariables(false) renders a variable that is not in the context as nothing rather than throwing. That last one is a trade: a misspelt variable name produces an empty gap on the page, not an error, and the template test does not catch it. When a value is missing from a page, compare the spelling in the template with the key in the Kotlin map before looking anywhere else.

        .loader(ClasspathLoader().apply { prefix = "templates/" })
        // Every {{ value }} is HTML-escaped. This is what makes rendering through templates safe.
        .autoEscaping(true)
        // Templates are re-read on every request, so edits show without a restart.
        .cacheActive(false)
        .strictVariables(false)
        .build()

C.3 Variables and the context
The context is a Kotlin Map<String, Any?> whose keys become variable names. The dot in task.title reads a map key, a public property or a getter, whichever the value has. renderTemplate adds isHtmx to every context, as Chapter 1 shows. The reference code hands templates maps of strings, booleans, numbers, lists and maps, built by the toPebbleContext() functions on Task and Page, so a template never calls a method to format a date or a number; the value arrives ready. A template that reaches into an object to format something is a template that breaks when the object changes.

title: Appendix C: Pebble
text:
C.4 Output and escaping
With autoEscaping on, a title of <b>bold</b> & "quoted" renders as <b>bold</b> & "quoted", inside an attribute as well as in text. The route test titles are escaped everywhere they appear checks exactly that. Escaping is HTML escaping. A value that goes into a URL needs the urlencode filter instead, as _pager.peb does with the query: a b&c becomes a+b%26c.

title: Appendix C: Pebble
text:
C.5 Control flow
if takes an expression and ends with endif; between them elseif and else are optional. Comparisons are ==, !=, <, >, <=, >=; and, or and not combine them; brackets group. A non-null, non-empty value is true, so {% if query %} in _list.peb means "if a filter is on". Tests follow is: is null, is not null, is empty, is defined.
for iterates a list and ends with endfor. The branch for an empty list is {% else %}, placed before {% endfor %}. The 2025 text taught {% empty %}, which is Django's tag; Pebble rejects it at parse time with Unexpected tag name "empty" and the template's name and line. Inside the loop, loop.index counts from zero, loop.revindex counts down to zero, loop.first and loop.last are booleans and loop.length is the size; loop.index0 is Twig and renders as nothing here.

D.1 The request header
This appendix collects the HTMX attributes and request patterns the book uses, with the accessible inline edit as the worked example.
HTMX is a script that reads hx- attributes on HTML elements, makes the request they describe, and swaps the HTML that comes back into the page (Big Sky Software, no date b). The reference code uses version 2.0.11, served by the application from static/js/htmx.min.js rather than a CDN. Nothing in the application depends on it: every form and link also carries the plain attributes a browser uses, and Chapter 6 is the check that they work. What follows is every attribute the code uses, where it uses it, and one worked example per pattern, included from a tag.
HTMX sends HX-Request: true on every request it makes, and that header is how the server knows to answer with a fragment. A URL that answers both ways sends Vary: HX-Request, as listTasks does in Chapter 5.

title: Appendix E: Accessibility testing
text:
E.1 The automated scan
This appendix is the method behind the audit in Chapter 4 and the regression checks in Chapter 10: four tests of ten minutes each, what each can and cannot find, and a checklist to run them from.
No single test finds everything. Deque's study of its own audit data found that automated rules detected 57 per cent of the issues found across the pages in its sample (Deque Systems, 2021); the rest were found by a person trying to use the page. The four parts below are ordered so that each catches what the one before cannot: the scan finds the mechanical faults, the keyboard finds what the scan cannot see, the screen reader finds what the keyboard cannot hear, and the contrast check measures what none of the other three do. Run all four on each state of the page that matters: the list, the edit form, and the page after a failed submit.
Open the page, open DevTools, choose the axe DevTools tab and scan the whole page; installing the extension is in Appendix A. Each result names the rule that fired, the element it fired on and the WCAG success criterion it maps to (W3C, 2023), with Deque's severity words critical, serious, moderate and minor, which are the tool's vocabulary and not the book's. Record the rule, the element and the criterion for each.
The scan is reliable on what can be decided from the markup alone: a form control without a label, an image without alt, text whose colour fails the ratio against a plain background, a missing lang attribute, duplicate id values, a heading sequence that skips a level. It cannot decide whether a label makes sense, where focus goes after a swap, whether a status message is announced, whether the page can be operated without a mouse, or whether anything works with JavaScript off. A scan with no violations is where the audit starts, not where it ends.
Scan the page in each of its states. The scan sees the document as it is at that moment; an error message that exists only after a failed submit is scanned only if you fail a submit first.

title: Appendix E: Accessibility testing
text:
E.2 Keyboard only
Put the mouse out of reach. Click once in the address bar and press Tab; the first stop should be the skip link, and Enter on it should move focus into the main content. Keep pressing Tab, and at each stop ask whether you can see where you are and whether the control does what it says with Enter or Space. Shift-Tab goes back. Complete every task the application supports, adding, editing, marking done, deleting, filtering and paging, without touching the mouse.
This finds a control that cannot be reached, which usually means a clickable element that is not a button or a link; a stop with no visible focus ring (2.4.7); an order that jumps about the page (2.4.3); a trap that focus can enter and not leave (2.1.2); and the one particular to this book, focus falling to the top of the document after an HTMX swap, so that the next Tab starts again from the skip link. It cannot tell you what a screen reader would announce, and it cannot measure contrast; a faint focus ring is a contrast question, below.
Record the order of the stops and any stop that failed, as a sentence or a short list; a screenshot of a focused control shows the ring. Ten minutes covers the application once; where a chapter changed a template, Tab through that state again.

title: Appendix E: Accessibility testing
text:
E.3 Screen reader
Use the screen reader for your platform, installed as Appendix A says. Three keys do most of the work in any of them: Tab moves focus between controls, H moves to the next heading, and one key switches between reading the page and operating a control.
NVDA: start it with Ctrl-Alt-N. Its modifier key is Insert, or Caps Lock if you chose that when installing. NVDA-Space switches between browse mode, in which H and F jump to the next heading and form field, and focus mode, in which keystrokes go to the control. Tools, Speech Viewer in the NVDA menu opens a window that logs everything spoken; copy from it for a transcript.
VoiceOver: Cmd-F5 toggles it; use it in Safari. Its modifier is Ctrl-Option, written VO. VO-Right Arrow reads the next item, VO-U opens the rotor, which lists headings, form controls and landmarks, and Tab moves focus as usual.
Orca: Super-Alt-S toggles it on GNOME. Its modifier is Insert on a desktop keyboard layout and Caps Lock on a laptop layout. Orca Modifier-A switches between browse mode and focus mode, and H moves to the next heading in browse mode. Orca has no speech log; write down what you hear as it is said.
With the reader running, do three things on the task list. Move through the headings and landmarks and listen for the structure. Tab to each control and listen for its name and role: "Edit, button" tells you the label works, and "button" alone tells you it does not. Submit the add form with an empty title and listen for the error, then with a valid title and listen for the status message; a live region that works is announced without your focus moving (4.1.3), and an error linked to its field with aria-describedby is read when you Tab back to the field (3.3.1).
This finds a control with no accessible name, a status message that is never announced, an error with no link to its field, an image whose alt text is its file name, and a reading order that differs from the visual one. It cannot find a faint focus ring, a low-contrast label, or anything about what a sighted person navigating by keyboard sees. Record what was announced, as text; a Speech Viewer log is the strongest form of this evidence, and a sentence of your own is acceptable where the tool has none.

title: Appendix E: Accessibility testing
text:
E.4 Contrast and zoom
Text needs a ratio of at least 4.5:1 against its background, large text 3:1, and controls and focus indicators 3:1 against what surrounds them (1.4.3 and 1.4.11). In Chrome, inspect the element and click the colour swatch in the Styles pane: the picker shows the ratio and whether it meets AA. In Firefox, the Accessibility panel's "Check for issues" menu has a contrast option that lists every failing element on the page. For a pair of values taken from a stylesheet, the WebAIM contrast checker takes two hex colours and gives the ratio (WebAIM, no date).
Then zoom to 200 per cent with Ctrl and plus until the browser says so, and narrow the window to about 320 CSS pixels (the device toolbar in Chrome DevTools, or Ctrl-Shift-M in Firefox for Responsive Design Mode). Nothing should be cut off and there should be no horizontal scrolling (1.4.10).
This finds grey placeholder text standing in for a label, a focus ring one shade from its background, and a layout that clips at zoom. It cannot find information carried by colour alone (1.4.1), which needs a person to notice that "red means overdue" has no other signal, and it guesses at the background when text sits over an image or a gradient.

title: Appendix F: Privacy and consent
text:
F.1 The principles
This appendix states the data-protection principles the book's peer studies follow, says what in them is personal data and what is not, and answers the questions students have asked about consent.
UK GDPR sets out seven principles for anyone processing personal data, and the Information Commissioner's Office publishes them in plain language (Information Commissioner’s Office, no date b, no date a). A peer study in a module is small, but it processes personal data, so the principles apply. What follows is each one as it bites on an interview from Chapter 2 or a pilot from Chapter 8.
Lawfulness, fairness and transparency. You have a lawful basis, which for these studies is the participant's consent, and the participant knows what you are collecting and why before you collect it. That is what the information sheet and the consent form are for; a participant who has not read one or heard the other has not consented.
Purpose limitation. The data is collected to evaluate the task list and is used for that and for the assessment that reports on it. It is not reused for something else later without going back to the participant.
Data minimisation. You collect what the evaluation needs and nothing more: no names, student numbers, email addresses, ages, degree programmes or anything about disability. The pseudonym and what the person did with the application are enough to answer the question.
Accuracy. Notes are written during the session, not reconstructed afterwards, and a quotation is marked as a quotation.
Storage limitation. The data is kept for the period the institution page states and then deleted, and the participant is told that period before they start.
Integrity and confidentiality. The consent forms, which carry initials or a signature, are kept where the institution page says and never in a repository. Pseudonymous notes and the metrics file may be committed to a private repository.
Accountability. You can show what you did: the information sheet and consent form you used are in research/, the consent log records each participant, and the retention period has a date.

title: Appendix F: Privacy and consent
text:
F.2 What is personal data
Personal data is information relating to an identified or identifiable living person (Information Commissioner’s Office, no date c). A name is personal data. So are a student number, an email address, a photograph, a voice recording, and a free-text note that says "the tall one from the Tuesday lab", because a reader who knows the cohort can work out who that is. Data about a person that cannot be tied to them is not.
A pseudonym such as P1 sits in between. On its own it identifies nobody. Together with the consent form that says who P1 was, it does. The ICO's position is that pseudonymised data is still personal data while the key exists, and the book's practice follows from that: the only key is the consent form, it is kept apart from the data and outside any repository, and it is destroyed first when the retention period ends. After that the notes and the metrics file are anonymous.
The metrics file is the clearest case. Its columns are defined in Chapter 7; they hold a timestamp, the pseudonym you set, a request code, a task code, what happened, how long the server took, a status code and the mode. The server does not record the address the request came from, the browser that made it, the title the participant typed, or the URL. Nothing in the file identifies a person. The one column that could be linked to one is the pseudonym, which only the consent form can resolve, so the file can be committed to a private repository and included in a submission as it stands.

title: Appendix F: Privacy and consent
text:
F.3 Withdrawal
A participant can stop at any point in a session and can ask afterwards for their data to be deleted, and the information sheet tells them how and until when. To honour a request, delete every row in the metrics file whose session_id is their pseudonym, delete their notes file, record the deletion in the consent log with the date, and destroy their consent form. A deletion from a git repository is a new commit, and the rows remain in the history. If the repository is private and will be deleted at the end of the retention period that is acceptable, and the information sheet should say so rather than promise that the data is gone.
Once findings have been written, a participant's contribution to "three of four participants" cannot be removed, which is why the sheet gives a withdrawal deadline. After it, you delete what still carries the pseudonym and leave the findings as they are.

title: Appendix F: Privacy and consent
text:
F.4 Questions students have asked
Can I test with someone who is not on the module? Yes, with consent and the same information sheet; peers are a convenience, not a rule. A participant under eighteen, or someone who depends on you, changes the risk, and you ask the ethics contact on the institution page first.
Can I record the session? No. Audio and video are not covered by a low-risk peer protocol and are personal data of the most identifying kind. Notes are enough.
Can I take a screenshot while the participant is working? Of the application, yes, provided it shows seed data and not the participant; Appendix J has the rules. Never of the person.
I wrote the participant's name in my notes. Replace it with the pseudonym now. If the notes were committed, say so in your reflection; a correction recorded is better than a secret.
Can I ask what course they are on, or whether they use a screen reader every day? Course, no; it adds nothing to the question. Assistive technology, only when it is what the task is about, and then record "uses a screen reader" and nothing about why.
Can I put the metrics file in my submission? Yes. The consent forms, no. The consent log, which holds pseudonyms and dates, yes.
Do I need ethics approval? The institution page says what the module has arranged for low-risk peer studies and whom to ask when a study falls outside it. Anything with recording, participants under eighteen, or questions about health or disability falls outside it.
Where do I find the data protection officer, the retention period and the data controller? On the institution page, and nowhere else in this book.

title: Appendix G: Participant information sheet
text:
G.1.1 What the study is for
The module teaches how to find out whether people can use an interface, by watching them use it. The evaluation measures how long tasks take and where they go wrong in two versions of the same page, one enhanced with JavaScript and one without. The results go into my coursework and into changes to the application.


G.1.2 What you will do
The session takes about twenty minutes. I will ask you to do up to five short tasks with the task list, such as adding a task or finding one, twice: once in each version. I will read each task out and watch, and a second student takes notes. After each task I will ask how confident you are that it worked, on a scale of one to five, and at the end I will ask three short questions about how it went. I will not help you during the tasks, because where people get stuck is what I need to find out, and you can skip a task or stop at any time.


G.1.3 What is recorded
The server that runs the application records each action it carries out: when, which task, whether it succeeded, and how long it took to respond. Those records are labelled with a code such as P1, which I assign, not with your name. The note-taker writes down what you do and anything you say, under the same code. Nothing is audio- or video-recorded, and no screenshot shows you.
I do not record your name, student number, email address, or anything about you other than what you do with the application. The only place your name or initials appear is the consent form, which is kept apart from the data and is not stored in any software repository.


G.1.4 What happens to the data
The records and the notes are kept in a private repository for the module and in my coursework submission, and are seen by me, my partner and the staff who mark the module. They are kept until [retention period] and then deleted. The consent form is kept until the same date and then destroyed. Findings in my coursework describe the participants together and do not identify anyone.


G.1.5 Your rights
Taking part is voluntary, and declining or stopping makes no difference to you on the module or anywhere else. You can stop during the session by saying so. You can ask me to delete your data up to [withdrawal deadline] after the session by giving me your code; after that your records have been combined with the others into findings that cannot be unpicked, but anything that still carries your code is deleted. You can ask to see what has been recorded under your code at any time.
The data controller is [data controller]. If you have a concern about how your data is handled, contact [data protection officer]; if you have a concern about the study, contact [ethics contact]. You also have the right to complain to the Information Commissioner's Office.


G.1.6 Before you decide
Ask me anything that is not clear. If you are happy to take part, I will ask you to initial the consent form and I will give you your code.

title: Appendix I: Evaluation metrics
text:
I.1 The metrics
This appendix defines each metric the book reports, says how it is computed from the metrics log, and ends with a quick reference. The log's columns are defined once, in Chapter 7; this page names columns and does not redefine them.
Time on task is the time between the participant being given a task and finishing it, in seconds. The log gives the finishing point exactly: the timestamp of the request that completed the task, which the evaluation plan names for each task. It gives the starting point only approximately: the timestamp of the previous request for that session, which is the end of the previous task or the page load before the first. Time on task from the log is the gap between those two, and it includes the facilitator reading the scenario and the participant thinking before acting. That is the same for every task and both modes, so the within-subject comparison is unaffected; the absolute numbers are a few seconds high and should be described as such. Report the median and the median absolute deviation, defined below, never the mean.
The ms column is not time on task. It is the time the server spent handling one request, in milliseconds, and in this application it is tens of milliseconds whatever the participant is doing. It answers one question only: whether a change you made slowed the server down. The 2025 text treated it as time on task and read a median of 1,899 milliseconds as nineteen seconds; it was under two seconds of server time and said nothing about the participant.
Error rate is the number of requests for a task that did not succeed, divided by the total number of requests for that task, within one mode. The numerator is the rows for that task code whose step is not success; in a pilot that means the validation_error rows, since the other two steps indicate a broken server rather than a participant. The denominator is all rows for that task code. State both numbers: "2 of 6" says what "0.33" hides, which is that one more error would have made it a half. Alongside the rate, report how many participants hit at least one error, which the session_id column gives, since one person failing three times and three people failing once are different findings.
Errors the server cannot see, such as deleting the wrong task, come from the notes and are reported separately with their own denominator, the number of attempts the note-taker observed. Do not add the two kinds together.
Completion is whether the participant reached the success criterion in the plan, judged by the facilitator: completed, completed after help, or not completed. The log cannot judge it, because a server that deleted the wrong task has succeeded. Report it as a count out of four for each task and mode.
Confidence is the participant's answer, from one to five, to "how confident are you that that worked?", asked after each task. Report the four answers for each task and mode as they are; with four numbers a median is already a summary, and a mean implies a precision the scale does not have. Low confidence after a completed task is a finding about feedback.
This book does not use a questionnaire such as SUS. Ten items at the end of a twenty-minute session with four people yield a score with nothing to compare it against.

title: Appendix I: Evaluation metrics
Appendix I: Evaluation metrics
text:
I.3 Reporting a within-subject comparison
Four participants did every task in both modes. For each task, the report is one table with a row per participant and columns for time on task in each mode and the difference, and a sentence under it. The sentence says how many of the four were faster in which mode and by how much, and names anyone who went the other way: "Three of four were faster with HTMX, by 4 to 11 seconds; P2 was 2 seconds slower." The same for errors: "Two of four made a validation error without JavaScript and none did with it; both errors were a blank title on the second edit." That is an effect described. It is not an effect tested. With four participants a hypothesis test has almost no power and a p-value says nothing a reader can use, so the book does not report one; it says what was seen, in whom, and how large it was, and lets the reader weigh it.
Say what the design cannot separate. Two participants did each order, so an order effect and a mode effect of similar size look alike; if the two who started without JavaScript were also the two who were slower with it, say so.
The example data at week-10 is between-subject, one mode per participant, and was generated before this design was settled; use it to practise the arithmetic, not as a model of the report.

title: Appendix J: Screenshot evidence
text:
J.1 What the image has to show
A screenshot is evidence when a reader can tell what page it shows, what state the page was in, and when. This appendix says how to take one that does, and how to keep people out of it.
Crop to the browser window, never the desktop, and keep three things inside the crop. The URL bar, so the reader can see the address and that it is your application. The state you are claiming: the error summary with its text legible, the status message after an add, the task gone from the list. And the footer of the application, which names the mode and the session code, so that a claim about the no-JavaScript path shows "no JavaScript" in the shot. Take the screenshot at 100% zoom, with the bookmarks bar hidden and no other tabs open, and save it as PNG; JPEG blurs text.
The date is not in the browser window, so it goes in the file name and in the caption where the shot is used. Name files YYYY-MM-DD-what-mode.png, for example 2026-11-18-add-error-summary-nojs.png, and keep them in evidence/. A caption says what the reader is looking at and what it shows: "The add form after a two-letter title without JavaScript; the error summary names the field and the typed text is kept."

title: Appendix J: Screenshot evidence
section: J.2 The accessibility tree and axe
text:
J.2 The accessibility tree and axe
A claim about what assistive technology is told needs a shot of the accessibility tree, not of the rendered page. In Chrome, select the element in the Elements panel of DevTools, open the Accessibility pane beside Styles, and screenshot the computed name, role and properties for that node; the button at the top right of the Elements panel switches on the full-page tree, which is the view for a claim about landmarks or heading order. In Firefox, the Accessibility panel in DevTools shows the same tree. Crop to the pane and the node, and increase the DevTools font size first if the text is small.
For an automated check, run the axe DevTools extension on the page and screenshot the results list with the rule names and counts visible, not the summary alone, so that a reader can see which rules failed and how many times. A shot of "0 issues" means little without the URL bar in the same image.

title: Appendix J: Screenshot evidence
text:
J.3 Keeping people out
A screenshot shows seed data, never a participant and never the participant's own machine. Hide the bookmarks bar, close other tabs, and check the window title and any file path in a terminal for a username before you save. Crop or blur rather than promise to; a shot with a name in it that reaches a submission is a breach, however small. The session code in the footer is a pseudonym and may stay.

title: Appendix K: Glossary
text:
Pre-print preview. A draft of Server-First HCI published for review. Every chapter is drafted; none is final. Corrections are welcome, and the preface says how the book is made.





This appendix defines the terms a reader of this book meets, each once, in alphabetical order.


Accessibility tree

The structure a browser builds from the page for assistive technologies: each element's role, name and state. A screen reader reads this, not the pixels, which is why a div styled as a button is not a button.

ARIA

Accessible Rich Internet Applications: HTML attributes such as role, aria-live, aria-describedby and aria-invalid that add meaning an element does not carry itself. The first rule of ARIA is to use the HTML element that already has the meaning.

aria-describedby

An attribute linking a control to the element whose text describes it, such as a hint or an error message, so that a screen reader reads the description when the control takes focus.

Audit

A review of a page against a standard, here WCAG 2.2, recording each defect against the success criterion it fails. Chapter 4 runs one.

Backlog

The CSV file of things to fix, one row each, with the evidence that justifies the row. Its columns are defined in Chapter 2 and nowhere else.

Browse mode and focus mode

The two states of a screen reader on a web page. In browse mode single keys move about the page, H to the next heading for instance; in focus mode keystrokes go to the control that has focus. The key that switches is in Appendix E.

Consent

A participant's agreement to take part after being told what will be recorded, kept and deleted, and that they can stop at any time. For a short interview between classmates spoken consent is enough; the form in Appendix H records that it was given.

Contrast ratio

The ratio between the luminance of text or a control and its background, from 1:1 to 21:1. WCAG asks 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text, controls and focus indicators.

Crit

A session in which one person presents one piece of work with its evidence and the audience responds to the evidence. Chapter 11.

Debrief

The conversation with a participant immediately after a pilot session, in which they say what was hard and why. Debrief notes carry the explanation that the metrics file cannot.

Error rate

The proportion of attempts at a task that ended in an error. Defined with the other metrics in Appendix I.

Error summary

A block at the top of a form, after a failed submit, listing each error with a link to the field it belongs to. The no-JS path relies on it because there is no live region to announce the error.

Evidence chain

The links from data to finding to fix to verification. Each link is a file, and each later link points back at the earlier one. The assessment is marked on whether the chains close.

Finding

A claim about what happened in the pilots, with its source: "participants without JavaScript failed the edit task in two of six attempts", with the rows that show it.

Focus

The one element on the page that receives keystrokes. Tab moves it forward and Shift-Tab back, and the focus ring shows where it is. A region that focus can enter and not leave is a keyboard trap. After a swap replaces the focused element, focus falls to the document unless something puts it elsewhere.

Fragment

A piece of HTML without the page around it, returned to an HTMX request and swapped into the page. The same template renders the fragment and the matching part of the full page.

HTMX

A JavaScript library that lets HTML attributes such as hx-get, hx-post, hx-target and hx-swap make requests and swap the returned HTML into the page. The attributes the book uses are in Appendix D.

HX-Request

The header HTMX sends with every request it makes. The server uses it to decide between returning a fragment and a full page; a plain form submission does not carry it.

Hypermedia

HTML that carries its own controls, links and forms, telling the browser what can be done next. The server returns hypermedia, not data for a client to render (Gross, Stepinski and Akşimşek, 2023).

Inclusion risk

The backlog column naming who is excluded by a defect: a person using a screen reader, navigating by keyboard, with low vision, under cognitive load or with a motor impairment.

Instrumentation

Code in the server that records one row per request to a metrics file, with the task, outcome, duration and mode, and nothing that identifies a participant. Chapter 7 builds it.

Job story

A need written as a situation, a motivation, an outcome and the constraint behind them: "When ..., I want to ..., so I can ..., because ...". Chapter 2 uses the form in place of personas and user stories.

Ktor

The Kotlin web framework the reference code uses for routing and responses.

Landmark

A region of the page with a role a screen reader can jump to: header, nav, main, footer. The skip link targets the main landmark.

Level A, AA and AAA

WCAG's three conformance levels. Each success criterion has one: A is the minimum, AA is what this book works to, and AAA is beyond its scope. The assessment fails a submission with a Level A failure remaining.

Live region

An element with aria-live, or a role such as status or alert, whose changes a screen reader announces without focus moving. The status message after adding a task is one; it must be the same element before and after a swap or the announcement is lost.

MAD

Median absolute deviation: the median of each value's distance from the median. A measure of spread that one slow participant does not dominate, which is why the book pairs it with the median rather than using the mean and standard deviation.

Median

The middle value when the values are sorted, with half above it and half below. One extreme value does not pull it as it pulls the mean.

Metrics file

The CSV the instrumentation writes, one row per request. Its columns are defined once, in the reference code, and Chapter 7 says where.

Needs-finding

Finding out what people are trying to do and what stops them, by asking and watching, before deciding what to build.

No-JS path

The way an interaction works with JavaScript off: a plain form submission, a server response and a full page. Every interaction in the book has one, and the HTMX path is an enhancement of it.

Out-of-band swap

An element in an HTMX response marked hx-swap-oob, which HTMX swaps into the page by its id in addition to the main target. The book uses it to update the status message from any response.

Parity

The requirement that every task that can be completed with JavaScript on can be completed with it off, ending in the same state. Chapter 6 checks it.

Partial

A template that renders one part of a page, named with a leading underscore, included by the page template and rendered on its own for a fragment. Chapter 5 introduces them.

Participant

A person who takes part in an interview or a pilot. The book's word for them; not "user", "subject" or "tester".

Participant code

The pseudonym a participant is known by in every file, P1, P2 and so on, assigned when consent is given. The only identity a participant has in the repository.

Pebble

The template engine the reference code uses to render HTML on the server. Its syntax is in Appendix C.

People-centred language

Naming the person and the situation rather than a label: "a person using a screen reader", not "a blind user". The situation is what the design has to work in, and it catches people the label would leave out.

Personal data

Anything that identifies a living person, alone or with other information: a name, an email address, a student number, a face, a voice. The repository holds none of it; Appendix F has the rules.

Pilot

A session in which a participant attempts set tasks on the instrumented application while you take notes. Chapter 8 runs them; the first pilots evaluate, and the re-pilot verifies a fix.

Portfolio

The README of your repository and the files it links to, at a named tag. Chapter 12.

Post/Redirect/Get

The pattern in which a successful form POST answers with a redirect, 303 See Other, to a GET, so that refreshing the page fetches again rather than submitting again. Every no-JS form in the book ends this way.

Prioritisation score

Impact plus inclusion minus effort, each on a small scale, used in Chapter 9 to rank findings. The simpler severity score in Chapter 2 is used before there are measurements.

Progressive enhancement

Building the page so that HTML alone does the job, then adding CSS and JavaScript for the browsers that run them, without the baseline depending on the additions (Government Digital Service, no date).

Regression check

A check run after a change to confirm that something that worked still works. The twenty for this application are in Chapter 10.

Re-pilot

A pilot run after a change, with the same tasks, to see whether the measurement moved.

Screen reader

Software that reads the accessibility tree aloud or to a braille display and lets a person navigate it from the keyboard. The book uses NVDA, VoiceOver and Orca, one per platform; installing them is in Appendix A.

Semantic HTML

Using the element that means the thing: button for an action, a for a link, label for a label, main for the main content. It gives the accessibility tree the right roles without ARIA.

Server-first

The approach in which the server renders every page and fragment and the browser is enhanced, not relied on. Chapter 1 makes the case.

Session cookie

The cookie that identifies a browser session to the server so that a participant's rows in the metrics file can be grouped. It carries a short random code, never a name.

Severity

The backlog's three-value column: high blocks a task or excludes a group, medium makes a task harder, low is cosmetic.

Skip link

The first link on the page, visible when focused, that moves focus past the header to the main content (WCAG 2.4.1).

Status message

Text that tells the person what just happened, such as "Task added", without taking their focus. WCAG 4.1.3 asks that it is announced to a screen reader, which the live region does.

Success criterion

One testable statement in WCAG, numbered like 2.1.1, with a level. A defect is recorded against the criterion it fails.

Tag

A name for one commit in git. The reference code has a tag for each state the book teaches from; your portfolio is submitted at a tag you name.

Task code

The short identifier the instrumentation writes for each task a participant attempts, so that rows can be grouped by task. The codes are defined once, in the reference code.

Time on task

How long a participant took to complete a task. Appendix I says how it is computed from the metrics file, and how it differs from the server's handling time for one request.

Validation

Checking submitted input on the server and returning the error with the form, in both paths. A check in the browser is an enhancement; the server's is the one that counts.

WCAG

The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, version 2.2, the W3C recommendation the book audits against (W3C, 2023).

title: Appendix L: Learning outcomes
text:
L.1 Foundations
This appendix states what a reader can do after each part of the book, and names the chapters that carry the evidence for each outcome.
The outcomes are written as things a reader can do, because that is what the chapters ask for and what the portfolio in Chapter 12 shows.
A module adopting the book maps them to its own outcome codes on the institution page (Chapter 15); the book itself carries none.
After Chapter 1 and Chapter 2, you can:

title: Appendix L: Learning outcomes
text:
Explain why a page rendered on the server that works with JavaScript off is the baseline, and what HTMX adds to it and what it does not.
Run a short needs-finding interview with spoken consent, keep notes in which the quotation and your reading of it are distinct, and write a need as a job story.
Build a backlog in which every row points at its evidence, and choose what to fix by severity and by who is excluded.
Collect the minimum of personal data, say where it is kept and when it is deleted, and keep to that.

title: Appendix L: Learning outcomes
text:
L.2 Building inclusively
After Chapter 3 to Chapter 6, you can:

Build an interaction that works by mouse, by keyboard and with a screen reader, in both the enhanced and the plain path, from one template.
Audit a page against WCAG 2.2 with an automated scan, a keyboard, a screen reader and a contrast check, and record each defect against its success criterion.
Fix a defect, show the diff, and show that the fix passes the check that found it.
Factor templates into partials so that a fragment and a page come from the same source, and give every view a URL that works without JavaScript.
Validate input on the server, return the error in both paths, and state the trade-offs of keeping parity.

title: Appendix L: Learning outcomes
text:
L.3 Evaluating
After Chapter 7 to Chapter 10, you can:

Write an evaluation plan with tasks and metrics, and instrument a server to log one row per event without recording anything that identifies a participant.
Run a pilot with consenting participants, debrief them, and keep notes from which a reader can trace a finding to its source.
Compute the median, the median absolute deviation and the error rate for each task in each condition, and turn a difference into a finding with its source.
Rank findings by impact, inclusion and effort, and say why the top one is top.
Make a change, run the regression checks, re-pilot, and assemble the chain from data to verification, reporting a change that did not help as plainly as one that did.

title: Appendix L: Learning outcomes
text:
L.4 Communicating
After Chapter 11 and Chapter 12, you can:

Present one evidence chain in five minutes, answer questions from the files rather than from memory, and respond to someone else's work by naming what you saw and what you could not see.
Write a portfolio in which every claim links to the data, code or screenshot behind it, state its limitations, and reflect in prose on what the evidence does not show.
